  1. (02, 03) Emotion is built, never announced: the emotion palette. APPROVED (Marc, Nov 10, 2026: "approve 133"). Rule: (a) The palette is a menu, not a checklist: the series plan names, for each episode, one main emotion the listener should feel and up to two supporting ones, chosen from the palette below to fit the story; it starts from its genre's set and may vary it. Only liking the protagonist is required in every story. Feelings should change across a series so episodes do not all feel the same. (b) The writer builds each named emotion with its setup and trigger; characters and the narrator never name the listener's feeling for them ("I was terrified", "it was heartbreaking"). (c) Every story builds liking for the protagonist in the first 3 minutes: one kind or brave act that costs them something, a clear want the listener can root for, and one small flaw. (d) The clarity reviewer checks only the emotions the plan chose; it lists each planned emotion with the line that sets it up and the line that triggers it, and flags any that is missing. Report-only until Marc reviews three stories with it, then Marc decides whether it blocks.

Palette (emotion: setup, then trigger):

  • Liking: the hero does a kind or brave thing that costs them, wants something simple, has one flaw; then the listener sees them keep trying.
  • Worry: the listener learns of a danger before the hero does, and the cost of failure is said plainly once; then the hero walks toward it.
  • Fear: the threat is close and real right now (a footstep in the room, a voice behind the door), described through what the hero hears and feels in short lines, with no way out yet; then the threat moves. Worry is about what might happen; dread is a slow build; fear is the moment the danger is here.
  • Stress: a clock, a narrowing choice, or a short pause before the answer; then the hero must act before they are ready.
  • Grief: the listener spends time with the person, place or thing first, in a small specific moment (a joke, a habit, a promise); then it is lost, and the scene stays with the loss before moving on.
  • Love and warmth: a small act of care that costs the giver something, shown not described; then it is returned or remembered later.
  • Hate (of the villain): the villain harms someone the listener already likes, on purpose, and shows no regret; then the villain gets away with it for now.
  • Bad feeling at a villain win: the villain takes something the listener has seen the hero care about; never a loss the listener was never shown.
  • Glee (villain caught): the villain's fall comes from something set up earlier (a clue, a skill, an ally the listener met), through the hero's own choice, never luck or rescue by others.
  • Relief: real danger, then a release that the hero earns, followed by a quiet moment.
  • Hope: a small win or a door opening after a low point, never a promise that everything will be fine.
  • Dread: small wrong details pile up (a sound, an object moved, someone who knows too much) before anything happens; then the thing the listener feared starts.
  • Longing: the listener sees what two people could have and what keeps them apart; then they almost reach it and are pulled back.
  • Jealousy: the listener sees what the hero values, then a rival gets near it; then the hero sees it too and wants to act on it.
  • Betrayal: a character earns the listener's trust over time with real help; then turns, and the earlier help now reads differently.
  • Shame: the hero hides one thing the listener knows about; then it comes out in front of someone whose opinion matters to them.
  • Awe: something large or strange is described through one concrete detail, never a list; then the hero goes quiet before it.
  • Amusement: a character's habit or way of talking is shown twice; then it pays off at the right moment, never at the cost of a serious beat.

Starting sets by genre (the plan may vary them):

  • Thriller or mystery: worry, fear, glee (stress as needed).
  • Romance (Pocket FM style): love and warmth, longing, jealousy, hope.
  • Horror: dread, fear, relief.
  • Family or grief drama: grief, love and warmth, hope.
  • Revenge: hate, bad feeling at a villain win, glee.
  • Betrayal or con story: betrayal, worry, glee.
  • Comedy or light drama: amusement, warmth, relief.
  • Science fiction or adventure: awe, worry, triumph (glee).

Audio tools for every emotion: pace (short lines speed up stress, long lines slow grief), a beat of silence before a hard line, and sound that belongs to the scene. Why: Marc, Nov 10, 2026: the listener should like the protagonist, feel bad when the villain succeeds, feel worry, and feel glee when the villain is caught, plus grief, stress, hate and love; stories will use different emotions; add the missing ones. A rule that only names feelings produces characters announcing them; a setup and trigger per emotion gives the writer steps and the reviewer something to check. Settles: nothing; builds on rule 47 (CANON-02, a lead to root for) and rules 14 and 25 (CANON-03, stakes). Fits decisions 129 to 131 (simpler plots leave room for feeling). Code: the series plan prompt (lib/series/continue-plan.ts: an "emotions" field per episode), the writer prompt (the palette and the no-announcing rule), and the clarity reviewer (lib/storyClarity.ts: an emotion check, report-only). Written into CANON-03 and CANON-02 as decision 133.
